schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch narrow the charge: the clause about Pharaoh's daughter means along with her rather than especially her, distinguishing her from the wives who turned Solomon's heart, so that what is blamed is only the loving of many foreign wives of nations Israel was forbidden to marry. Ellicott sorts the five nations into three kindred to Israel and of the stock of Abraham and two of the old Canaanitish stock, notes that the prohibition of the Law properly attached to the last alone though its reason applied equally to the rest, and observes that no Egyptian idolatry is anywhere mentioned.
Clarke refuses to exempt the Egyptian marriage, holding that she too was a strange woman and an idolater, and that the common opinion of her conversion to the Jewish religion rests on no evidence.
Gill puts the charge in a word, that the love was lustful and not lawful, and of women who were not only foreign but not his lawful wives.

Henry treats the whole chapter as a fall and asks how the beauty of Israel could come to it, tracing the beginning to the very thing his mother had cautioned him against and his father had first stumbled over, and drawing the rule that lesser sins made bold with open the door to greater.

debates.question: Does the blame reach the marriage with Pharaoh's daughter?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew as setting her alongside rather than among the offending wives, so the censure passes her by; Clarke will not allow the distinction, holding her an idolater and the first of the strange women, with nothing to show she ever became a proselyte.

outliers.view: Presses the danger of example over the danger of appetite: David had multiplied wives too much, which perhaps made Solomon presume it lawful, and one bad act of a good man may be of more pernicious consequence than twenty of a wicked man.

themes: he loved many strange women
along with the daughter of Pharaoh
surely they will turn away your heart
the way of sin is down-hill

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch call the figures round numbers approximating to the reality, covering every woman received into the harem across the whole reign rather than all present at once, which leaves room for the smaller count of queens and concubines given elsewhere. Ellicott describes the harem of an Eastern king as an adjunct of magnificence in which the relation of the wives is little more than nominal, then goes further than the rest and allows that the numbers, extraordinarily large and disproportionate between the superior and inferior ranks, may point to a corruption of ancient date.
Gill calls the number prodigious and suggests that these might not all have been for use but for state, after the manner of the eastern monarchs.

Clarke wonders how so many of the blood royal could be got from the surrounding nations and supposes the daughters of noblemen and generals included, explains the concubines as wives of the second rank whose offspring could not inherit, and then refuses every excuse built on the custom of the East.

debates.question: Are the numbers to be taken as they stand?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch take them as round totals across the reign and so reconcilable with the other account; Ellicott finds them excessive by comparison and disproportionate in themselves, and holds the text may be corrupt, though the corruption must then be very old.

outliers.view: Turns the question back on the reader, asking in what state a man must be who has a thousand women when we scarcely allow the fear of God to one with a second wife, and closing on the rule that as we should not condemn what God justifies, we should not justify what God condemns.

themes: seven hundred wives, princesses
three hundred concubines
his wives turned away his heart

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe a season in which the flesh gained the supremacy over the spirit, so that the heart was no longer wholly with the Lord, the word meaning entirely devoted as David's had been, who sinned grievously but never fell into idolatry. Ellicott reads the same clause as implying senile feebleness, possibly the premature result of indulgence, and then argues that the apostasy was not a forsaking of the worship of God at all but an eclectic adoption of various forms of faith as phases of reverence to one Supreme Power, the natural fruit of overweening confidence in his own wisdom and of absolutely despotic power.

Gill puts Solomon near sixty at the time, reckoning back from the age of the son who succeeded him, and takes the lateness as an aggravation: in old age, when long experience might have made him wiser and less lustful, this was what he came to.

debates.question: What kind of apostasy was this?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch describe a divided heart measured against David's undivided one; Ellicott denies outright that the worship of God was forsaken and diagnoses a philosophic spirit holding no creed but condescending to all, perhaps helped along by the policy of conciliating subject races.

outliers.view: Finds a kinship between the belief that all worships are true and the weary conviction that all things are vanity, and compares the Roman Empire's readiness to honour every religion once faith in its own had died out.

themes: when Solomon was old
his heart was not perfect
as was the heart of David his father

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch limit the recorded idolatry to the building of altars on which the foreign wives offered, noting that Solomon is not said to have sacrificed himself, yet refuse to let that excuse him, since even building altars for idols was a participation irreconcilable with fidelity to the Lord; they make Astarte the chief female deity of the Canaanite tribes, follow her worship from Tyre to Carthage, and insist Milcom is not to be confounded with Molech. Ellicott derives the name from a root that became the Greek and Latin words for a star, notes that this is the first place where it stands in the singular and is limited to the goddess of the Zidonians, and calls the worship one of chartered licence.

Gill supplies the local connection, that Solomon was enticed by the Zidonian women he had and that the Phoenician histories make him the husband of a daughter of Hiram, and identifies Ashtoreth flatly with the Venus of the Greeks, citing an ancient writer who says the Sidonians took her for the moon.
Clarke takes the harder line, that Solomon burnt incense to these gods himself and seems to have gone as far in iniquity as it was possible.

debates.question: Is Milcom the Molech to whom children were offered?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch insist the two must not be confounded; Ellicott holds Milcom probably only a variety of the well-known name, arguing that it is a general title signifying king as Baal signifies lord, and pointing to the same rite of passing children through the fire recorded of the Carthaginians.

outliers.view: Notes the horned Ashteroth preserved in the ancient name of a city in Bashan, and reads the earlier plural Ashtaroth beside the Baalim as meaning simply the gods and goddesses of idolatry in general.

themes: Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians
Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites
went after Ashtoreth

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the siting its meaning: the high place stood on the mount of Olives, part of which still traditionally bears the name of the Mount of Offence, facing and rivalling the Temple on the opposite height, while the actual sacrifice to Molech belonged separately to the valley of the son of Hinnom. Keil and Delitzsch answer by arithmetic how many altars the phrase about all his foreign wives requires, holding that three sufficed, since the Hittites appear to have worshipped Astarte with the Sidonians and the Edomites Milcom, and the Old Testament names gods of the Edomites in only one place and gives no names there.

Gill has Solomon order the building, or suffer it to be built, at the instigation of his Moabitish women, on the hill afterwards called the mount of corruption, and explains why it did not stop at one: having done it for one wife he could not refuse another without greatly disobliging her. He glosses the doing of evil in the sight of the Lord by saying that idolatry is what it names, and that nothing is more provoking to him.
Clarke identifies the hill in five words to the same effect as the rest.

outliers.view: Explains the multiplication of shrines by court politics rather than by religion: once the first wife had her altar, refusal to the next was impossible, and so it went on for as many as asked.

themes: the hill that is before Jerusalem
so did he for all his strange wives
he went not fully after the Lord

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the stress on the two direct visions is deliberate, since they contrast with the usual indirect revelation through the prophets and so carried peculiar privilege and responsibility. Keil and Delitzsch put the weight where an early commentator put it, that God had appeared to warn him in person and had not merely caused him to be warned by prophets.

Henry turns the appearances into the first of two counts, the basest ingratitude, since God had appeared once before the temple was begun and once after it was dedicated and keeps account of such visits whether we do or not; the second count is wilful disobedience, this being the very thing concerning which God had expressly commanded him, and he generalises it to all who have dominion over men and forget God's dominion over them.

Clarke explains why the fall had to be recorded at all, since unmarked it would have had a fatal effect on the morals of mankind, and then separates the guilt of an act from the desert of the man: the act is the same in God's sight, but circumstances aggravate, and Solomon knew better, had seen the vanity of idolatry, had been visited twice and had watched the promises fulfilled.
Gill states the aggravation plainly, that the command had been particularly given to Solomon and he had been warned to observe it.

outliers.view: Concludes that Solomon deserved more punishment for worshipping Ashtaroth than any of the Sidonians who performed precisely the same acts, because they had never known the true God and he had been fully acquainted with him.

themes: the Lord was angry with Solomon
which had appeared unto him twice
he kept not that which the Lord commanded

schools.summary: Gill supplies the missing channel of the sentence, that it came not in a vision as before but through a prophet, probably the Ahijah who appears later in the chapter, and is careful to say that the sparing of one tribe rests not on David's merits but on the promises made to him.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the shape of the threat with its two limitations: the kingdom shall be torn away and given to a servant, yet not in Solomon's lifetime, for his father's sake, and not the whole of it, since one tribe remains to his son.

Clarke reads the message as another opening rather than a closing, asking whether Solomon might not yet have recovered himself and whether there was not mercy in it to be sought and found, and then traces a longer purpose through both reservations: the line of the Messiah had to be preserved, so tribe and regal right alike were kept for the true David's sake.

Henry finds the sentence exactly fitted to the crime, that one who revolted from God should see part of his kingdom revolt from his family, and one who gave God's glory to the creature should see his crown given to his servant.

outliers.view: Reads Jerusalem as a type of the true Church, so that the old city had to be preserved in the hands of that tribe until the true David should establish the New Jerusalem in the same land, and exclaims at the series of providences required to do it.

themes: forasmuch as this is done of thee
I will surely rend the kingdom from thee
for David my servant's sake
one tribe to thy son

schools.summary: Gill states the arrangement plainly: though God did not take the kingdom from Solomon for his sin, he chastised him with the rod of men as he had said he would, suffering one and then another to rise up and disturb his peace in his old age.

Clarke plays on the Hebrew word for adversary and gets a biography out of it, contrasting the message to Hiram that there was no satan and all the kingdom at peace with the three satans that rise once Solomon has turned away; and on the Edomite war he reckons that Joab exterminated all the males within six months and notes an old version reading not to bury the slain but to take their spoils.

Henry measures the men against the king, finding them inconsiderable and incapable of doing anything worth notice had Solomon not first made God his enemy, and adds two observations that govern the rest of the chapter: that God stirred both of them up while they acted from ambition or revenge, and that both enmities had their origin in David's conquests, so that Solomon inherited his father's quarrels with his father's dominion.

Ellicott makes Hadad a title rather than a name, most often borne by the kings of Syria though given here to a member of the royal house of Edom, and reports the authorities who take it for a Syriac title of the sun, assumed either as claiming descent from the sun-god or as an appellation of splendour; on the war he collates the accounts, which ascribe the victory variously and here bring David himself into it. Keil and Delitzsch note the same name on a pre-Mosaic king of Edom and refuse the conjecture that this Hadad was his grandson.

debates.question: How do the accounts of the Edomite war fit together?
debates.positions: Ellicott finds the victory ascribed to Joab in one record and to Abishai in another while David takes part here, and suggests David completed a conquest Joab had begun; Keil and Delitzsch confine themselves to the name Hadad and reject the genealogical conjecture built on the earlier king of that name.

outliers.view: If God be on our side we need not fear the greatest adversary, but if he be against us he can make us fear the least, and the very grasshopper shall be a burden.

themes: the Lord stirred up an adversary
Hadad the Edomite
of the king's seed in Edom
until he had cut off every male

schools.summary: Clarke will not let the English obscure the age, insisting the words mean a little boy, apprehensive of his danger and able to escape with his father's servants, not an infant, and traces the route from Midian to Paran in the south of Idumea, where the party gathered recruits before going straight to Egypt.
Gill fixes the moment of the flight against the previous verse, that Hadad got away while Joab was burying the slain.

Ellicott stops on the oddity of the first stage, since the flight should have started in Edom itself, and offers either a branch of the Midianites settled between Edom and the desert or a city of that name near the Gulf of Elath to which the old Greek version expressly refers; Paran he places in the Sinaitic region, inhabited then by an independent race from which the fugitives enlisted support. Keil and Delitzsch say what the support was for, that men were taken from Paran as guides through the desert, and describe the reception in Egypt as a settlement, with a house, maintenance and land to cultivate.

outliers.view: Argues on chronological grounds that this Pharaoh was not the king who became Solomon's father-in-law, and suggests that jealousy of the growing power of Israel prompted the welcome, as it afterwards prompted the welcome of Jeroboam.

themes: Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites
they arose out of Midian
and came to Egypt

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe an adoption rather than a kindness, with the sister of Pharaoh's own wife given to Hadad and the son weaned in the royal palace and brought up among Pharaoh's sons; they take the question about what he lacked as a pure expression of love and attachment carrying an implied request that he stay, print his answer that he lacked nothing but must be let go, and note that the release, though not recorded, must be supplied. Ellicott presses the two proper names and finds nothing behind either in history or on the Egyptian monuments, but reads the weaning in the house of Pharaoh, no doubt with the customary festival, as marking the child's admittance into the royal family.

Gill supplies a reason for the favour from the man himself, his comely personage and princely qualities and good behaviour as he grew, reads the son's name as signifying stealth and perhaps commemorating Hadad's own stealthy escape, notes that the death of princes is soon known abroad and especially of a king of David's fame, and spreads Pharaoh's question into its parts, equipage, provisions, honour, favour.

Clarke marks what Hadad did not say, that it does not appear he avowed his real intention, since at this time there must have been peace between Israel and Egypt, Solomon having married the daughter of Pharaoh.

outliers.view: Treats the silence of the Egyptian record as itself worth stating: neither the queen's name nor the son's can be found in history or on the monuments.

themes: Hadad found great favour
the sister of his own wife
what hast thou lacked with me
howbeit let me go in any wise

schools.summary: Gill places the second adversary in the opposite quarter, one from the north as the other was from the south, and limits the closing phrase with care, that Rezon was an adversary not through the whole of Solomon's life but through all his days from his first going into idolatry to the end of it.

Clarke reads both adversaries as the exact fulfilment of Nathan's older threat of chastening with the rod of men, makes Rezon one of the captains of the king of Zobah who escaped with his men after the defeat, lived as is supposed by plunder, seized Damascus and was driven out by David, and recovered it after Solomon's defection when he found that God had departed from Israel; he adds that some think Hadad and Rezon the same person.

Ellicott takes the name to signify prince, as might naturally mark the founder of a new power, connects it with a king of Damascus named later, reports the tradition Josephus takes from Nicolaus of Damascus that ten generations of Syrian kings bore the name Hadad and judges it an official title, and dates an independent power at Damascus to the later days of Solomon, since David had put governors there and made its people tributary. Keil and Delitzsch have Rezon flee his lord for some unassigned reason while that king was at war with David, gather a company from the fugitives, and take Damascus towards the close of David's reign or after it.

debates.question: When and how did Rezon establish himself at Damascus?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch have him flee before his lord's complete overthrow, collect fugitives, and seize the city late in David's reign or after; Clarke makes him a captain who took Damascus, was expelled by David, and recovered it only once Solomon had fallen away.

outliers.view: Registers a difficulty in the text itself: the recurrence to Hadad in the clause about the mischief he did is curiously abrupt, and on the general reading of the old Greek version Edom must be substituted for Syria, a slight change in the Hebrew.

themes: Rezon the son of Eliadah
he abhorred Israel
beside the mischief that Hadad did

schools.summary: Gill reports the Jewish writers who made Jeroboam the Sheba who had rebelled under David, and gives the two answers a rabbi returned, that the one was a Benjamite and the other an Ephraimite, and that Sheba's head had been thrown over the wall to Joab.

Ellicott corrects the description, since the word rendered Ephrathite usually means an inhabitant of Bethlehem but is here another form of Ephraimite, places the town in the Jordan valley and notes a Greek manuscript with a different name, reads the widowed mother and the title of servant as marking the dependent condition from which royal favour raised the future rebel, deflates the phrase about a mighty man of valour into a statement of capacity rather than of war, and dates the building of Millo some twenty years into the reign, when delight in magnificence grew and with it the burdens of the people.

Henry turns the same details kinder and then didactic: Providence made up to the widow the loss of a husband in an active and ingenious son, and Solomon's wisdom lay in employing proper persons, advancing an industrious young man who minded his business and did it with all his might until he was set over the burden of the house of Joseph.

Clarke locates the disaffection on a building site, where Jeroboam superintended the works at Millo and distinguished himself, and where Solomon, growing profane and with it tyrannical, changed his conduct toward Israelite labour, so that in all probability the seeds were sown there.

outliers.view: Draws the maxim that industry is the way to preferment, seest thou a man diligent in his business, he shall stand before kings, and then compares three reigns: Saul took the valiant man, Solomon preferred the industrious, but David's eyes were upon the faithful in the land.

themes: Jeroboam the son of Nebat
his mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman
a mighty man of valour
the charge of the house of Joseph

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the appearance of the prophet the event itself: in Ahijah prophecy emerges from the abeyance that overshadowed it during the greatness of the monarchy, when Nathan appears chiefly as counsellor, Solomon himself receives the visions, and the king alone is prominent at the consecration of the Temple; here begins a line of prophets resuming a paramount influence like that of Samuel. He treats the torn garment as Ahijah's own and sets it among the symbolical acts of later prophecy, whose object is to arrest attention and provoke the question what these things are to us, comparing Saul's rending of Samuel's mantle. Keil and Delitzsch fix the date, that at that time means while Jeroboam was overseer and not after the rebellion had begun, since the whole account explains the earlier statement that he lifted up his hand against the king.

Clarke adds that Ahijah was one of those who wrote the history of the reign, and that it is supposed to have been by him that God spoke twice to Solomon and delivered the sentence earlier in this chapter; on Jeroboam's errand out of the city he declines to guess.

Gill offers two guesses at the errand, either that Jeroboam was going to enter on his new office or returning to the country after paying in the revenues, and notes that the wording of the rending looks as though the garment were Jeroboam's own, newly got to appear before the king in, though the sense may be that the prophet took hold of his own.

debates.question: Whose garment did Ahijah tear?
debates.positions: Gill allows that the wording suggests Jeroboam's new garment while admitting the prophet may have taken hold of his own; Ellicott treats it as Ahijah's own and reads the act as a symbol in the prophetic manner.

outliers.view: Let the message supply its own ground: the tribes are given away because the people have forsaken God for the goddess of the Zidonians and the gods of Moab and Ammon, and have not walked in his ways as David did.

themes: Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the way
he had clad himself with a new garment
rent it in twelve pieces
take thee ten pieces

schools.summary: Clarke spells out the arithmetic of the torn garment piece by piece, the garment standing for the kingdom, the twelve pieces for the twelve tribes and the ten for the tribes that would form the kingdom of Israel ruling in Samaria as distinguished from Judah ruling in Jerusalem; he reduces the promise of a light alway to a single sense, that David's posterity should never fail and the regal line never become extinct, and takes it as a reference to the Messiah, who was not only David's light but a light to enlighten the Gentiles; and he infers from the clause about all that his soul desired that Jeroboam had already affected the kingdom and was watching for his opportunity.

Gill reads the ten pieces the same way and accounts for the remainder by reckoning Judah and Benjamin as one tribe, marks that the loss falls not on Solomon's hand but on his son's, offers three senses of the light promised in Jerusalem, a kingdom as one old version renders it, an illustrious prince shining in royal majesty to guide and comfort the people, or an honour to David's family and a means of continuing the pure worship of God in the temple, and keeps to the plain sense of the taking, that God would raise Jeroboam from the low estate he was in.

debates.question: What does the promise of a light alway hold out?
debates.positions: Gill spreads it across three readings, a kingdom, a shining successor, or the continuance of the temple worship as an honour to David's house; Clarke narrows it to the unfailing line and reads it directly of the Messiah.

outliers.view: Reads the promise as a boundary set to ambition, God telling Jeroboam by the prophet what he shall have and what he shall not, to prevent him from seizing the whole kingdom to the prejudice of the spiritual seed of David.

themes: I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand
that David my servant may have a light alway
thou shalt reign according to all that thy soul desireth

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the terms of the conditional promise as they stand, a sure house built as David's was if Jeroboam will hearken and walk and keep the statutes, and then refuse to let the prophecy excuse the rebellion: the account of the flight continues the earlier statement that he lifted up his hand against the king, so he plainly organised a revolt, and plainly did so only after being told he would reign over ten tribes once Solomon was dead, which did not justify the attempt. Ellicott agrees and supplies a motive on each side, the knowledge of the promise exciting the old king's jealousy and Jeroboam's impatience driving him to clutch at royalty, with the Greek addition describing him as collecting three hundred chariots; he identifies Shishak with a king of the monuments whose accession the Egyptian traditions fix near nine hundred and eighty years before Christ, and turns the absence of the usual generic title into evidence, since Shishak founded a new dynasty rather than continuing the old royal line.

Clarke says what became of the condition, that God would have continued Jeroboam's posterity on the throne had he not forfeited the promises by his wickedness, reads the closing words about affliction as a horizon rather than a reprieve, the seed of David in distress until the Messiah come to order the throne in judgment, quotes a rabbi to the same effect, and notes that this is the first time an Egyptian king is met by proper name rather than by the common title.

Gill states the cause of the affliction plainly, the idolatry Solomon had been guilty of and connived at, and calls the attempt on Jeroboam's life another instance of Solomon's folly, since he had himself been assured the kingdom should be rent away and given to his servant.

debates.question: Who is the Shishak that sheltered Jeroboam?
debates.positions: Ellicott identifies him with a named king of the Egyptian monuments and calls the identification an important point in Biblical chronology; Clarke rejects the identification with the conqueror renowned in Greek history, holding that he lived long before Solomon's time.

outliers.view: Explains the attempted murder as an attempt at evasion, that Solomon thought by this means to prevent the punishment due to his crimes.

themes: I will build thee a sure house
I will for this afflict the seed of David
but not for ever
Jeroboam fled into Egypt, unto Shishak

schools.summary: Gill weighs three possibilities for the book of the acts of Solomon, written by the king himself as Kimchi suggested though not now in being, compiled by a chronologer he employed, or assembled out of several prophets; on the length of the reign he cites Eupolemus, who allowed Solomon only fifty-two years of life, notes the common Jewish tradition of accession at twelve and refutes it from the age of Rehoboam, and sets against it the eighty years of reign given by Josephus.

Henry takes the middle option on the lost book, a court historiographer whose annals the inspired writer quarried for what God saw fit to transmit to the church, and closes the reign in his own manner: Solomon followed his fathers to the grave and was buried with honour in David's burying-place, his son followed him to the throne, and his reign was as long as his father's though his life was not, for sin shortened his days.

Clarke settles the authorship from the parallel record, which puts the acts in the book of Nathan, the prophecy of Ahijah and the visions of Iddo, supposes both Kings and Chronicles composed from these now lost originals, calls the eighty years of Josephus sufficiently absurd, prefers the reckoning that makes Solomon eighteen at accession and fifty-eight at death, and adds that given the excess in which he lived this life was as long as could reasonably be expected.

Ellicott reads the prophets of the parallel record as annalists and apportions the reign among them, Nathan's book covering the early years, Ahijah's most of the later reign, Iddo's visions touching the close only incidentally, and observes that Kings is visibly a compilation differing from part to part in style and detail, drawn here from a temple record and there from official archives; he calls the exact equality with David's forty years curious but refuses to treat the figures as round numbers. Keil and Delitzsch observe that Solomon was not more than twenty at his accession and so did not live to a great age, and leave the question of his repentance where Scripture leaves it, while allowing that if the leading thoughts of Ecclesiastes are traceable to him they would be evidence of conversion, or at least that he discovered at the last how empty earthly aims are.

debates.question: How long did Solomon live, and how long did he reign?
debates.positions: Gill reports Eupolemus at fifty-two years of life and refutes the tradition of accession at twelve from Rehoboam's age; Clarke and Ellicott both reject the eighty-year reign of Josephus, Ellicott ascribing it to a textual error or a confusion of the two reigns, while Keil and Delitzsch fix the accession at not more than twenty.

outliers.view: Decline to answer the question the older commentators argued at length, whether Solomon turned again to the Lord with all his heart, holding that it cannot be ascertained from the Scriptures.

themes: the book of the acts of Solomon
forty years
he slept with his fathers

schools.summary: Gill's whole note on the last verse is that Solomon died as his fathers did.

Clarke uses the same words to open an essay on the character of the king, the longest thing in the chapter and the frankest. He died almost in the flower of his age and, it appears, unregretted, his government no blessing to Israel and its exactions the foundation of the schism that followed. On the bright side Clarke sets the boy loved by the Lord and named by divine authority, the honouring of his father's charge about the temple though the architectural knowledge was Hiram's, the commerce learned from the Tyrians and afterwards let dwindle, the early piety proved by the prayer for wisdom and the prayer at the dedication, the one surviving poem of a thousand and five, and the lost natural history. On the reverse he lists the affinity with Pharaoh's daughter as the first means of drawing the heart away, the oppressive taxation forced by the building, the house of the forest of Lebanon consuming nearly thirteen years against the temple's seven, the inauspicious death of Adonijah, the seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and the shrine built for every foreign worship; and he traces the taxation forward to the separation, the wars, the captivity and the vanished ten tribes.

outliers.view: Refuses the comfortable conjecture that Ecclesiastes proves a late repentance, observing that the text which reports the apostasy reports the death with no word of turning between them.

themes: Solomon slept with his fathers
buried in the city of David his father
Rehoboam his son reigned in his stead
